title: Multiply Digit Strings
statement:
Two non-negative integers are given as decimal strings a and b. Return their product, also as a decimal string, with no leading zeros (the product zero is "0").

The inputs can be 200 digits long. You may not turn either whole string into a number: no Number(a), parseInt, BigInt, or Python int(a). Work digit by digit, the way you multiply on paper.

examples.why: 45 · 7 = 315 and 45 · 20 = 900, and 315 + 900 = 1215. Each partial product must be shifted by its digit's place.
The product is zero. A digit array of all zeros must collapse to one "0", not "0000".
Twenty digits is beyond what a plain number holds exactly: Number(a) * 3 comes out as 300000000000000000000.

constraints: a and b contain only digits
No leading zeros, except the number 0 itself
hints: Multiply the way you learned at school, but think about where each single-digit product lands.
The digit at position i of a (from the left) times the digit at position j of b contributes to position i + j + 1 of a result array of length a.length + b.length.
Add every digit-pair product into that slot first, then sweep once from the right turning each slot into a digit and passing the rest as carry. Skip leading zeros at the end.

explain.intuition:
The product of an m-digit and an n-digit number has at most m + n digits, so allocate an array of that length. Now look at one pair: digit a[i] times digit b[j]. Counting from the right, a[i] sits at place m − 1 − i and b[j] at place n − 1 − j, so their product belongs at place (m − 1 − i) + (n − 1 − j). In a left-to-right array of length m + n that is index i + j + 1.

So add every digit-pair product into slot i + j + 1, without worrying about carries yet. Slots can grow past 9; that is fine. One sweep from the right then fixes everything: keep slot % 10, push floor(slot / 10) into the slot on its left. It is long multiplication with the carrying done once at the end. Why not just use BigInt? Because an interviewer asking this wants to see the paper method, and the problem forbids it.
steps: Let m = a.length, n = b.length and make slots, an array of m + n zeros.
For every i and j, add digit(a[i]) · digit(b[j]) to slots[i + j + 1].
Sweep k from m + n − 1 down to 1: add floor(slots[k] / 10) to slots[k − 1] and keep slots[k] % 10.
Skip leading zeros, keeping at least one digit, and join the rest into a string.
pitfalls: Converting the strings with Number. Past about 16 digits the low digits are wrong, as in the third example.
Returning "000" for a zero product. Strip leading zeros but keep one digit.
Placing the pair product at i + j instead of i + j + 1. Every digit shifts one place and the top slot overflows.

solutions.title: Add shifted partial products as strings
solutions.idea: Multiply a by one digit of b at a time to get a partial product string, pad it with zeros for its place, and add it to a running total with string addition.

solutions.title: One slot per digit place
solutions.idea: Accumulate a[i] · b[j] into slot i + j + 1 of an (m + n)-length array, then resolve all carries in one right-to-left sweep.

followups: Each slot can collect up to min(m, n) products of 81. When could that overflow a 32-bit int, and how would you guard against it?
Karatsuba multiplies two n-digit numbers in about O(n^1.58). What is the idea in one sentence?
Support negative inputs with a leading '-'.
